question: How does fire spread on fabric in microgravity?
answer:
In microgravity, ventilation airflow strongly enhances flames, and fires in low-speed airflows may preferentially spread into the oncoming airflow, which is opposite to normal gravity [A Researcher's Guide to International Space Station Combustion Science (2015) · nasa.gov/missions/station/a-researchers-guide-to-combustion-science]. Materials are also easier to ignite in low gravity due to reduced natural convective cooling from the fuel surface [A Researcher's Guide to International Space Station Combustion Science (2015) · nasa.gov/missions/station/a-researchers-guide-to-combustion-science]. Theory suggests flame spread over thin fuels in quiescent microgravity is influenced by how the flow field affects the overlap of thermal and species fields [A Researcher's Guide to International Space Station Combustion Science (2015) · nasa.gov/missions/station/a-researchers-guide-to-combustion-science]. 

In microgravity glovebox experiments, fabric fuels—including Nomex and a 75% cotton and 25% fiberglass blend measuring 1 to 2 cm—were tested under forced airflows reaching up to 40 cm/s in opposed or concurrent directions across 122 test rows [PSI-26 · doi:10.60555/58h4-dy80]. These experiments measured flame spread rate, size, shape, color, and flame quenching [PSI-26 · doi:10.60555/58h4-dy80]. 

The provided sources do not cover specific numerical flame spread rates for fabrics in microgravity.

question: Which experiments tested oxygen levels above 30%?
answer:
Based on NASA PSI data, four experiments tested oxygen levels above 30% [PSI comparison table: oxygen · DOIs per row]. 

PSI-159 ACME CFI-G tested oxygen levels ranging from 12% to 85% O2 [PSI comparison table: oxygen · DOIs per row]. PSI-10 ACME/Flame Design tested oxygen levels from 19.8048% to 84.9978% O2 [PSI comparison table: oxygen · DOIs per row][PSI-10 · doi:10.60555/w4zy-bt45]. PSI-20 ACME BRE tested oxygen levels from 21% to 40% O2 [PSI comparison table: oxygen · DOIs per row][PSI-20 · doi:10.60555/vb93-3y72]. PSI-69 FLEX tested oxygen levels between 12% and 34% O2 [PSI comparison table: oxygen · DOIs per row].

question: How was smoke detection tested on the ISS, and why does it matter?
answer:
Smoke detection on the ISS was tested using the Dust Aerosol Measurement Feasibility Test, the Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment (SAME), and SAME-Reflight (SAME-R) [A Researcher's Guide to International Space Station Combustion Science (2015) · nasa.gov/missions/station/a-researchers-guide-to-combustion-science][PSI-101 · doi:10.60555/2np7-jv14][PSI-102 · doi:10.60555/gd4k-8h62]. SAME examined solid fuels such as Teflon, Kapton, silicone rubber, lampwick, and dibutyl phthalate across 8 experimental test rows at airflows of 5–10 cm/s [PSI-102 · doi:10.60555/gd4k-8h62]. SAME-R tested fuels including Pyrell foam, DBP, and Kapton across 109 experimental test rows [PSI-101 · doi:10.60555/2np7-jv14]. Measurements used smoke detectors, ionization detectors, DustTrak, thermal precipitators, TEM grids, video cameras, and thermophoretic soot samplers [PSI-101 · doi:10.60555/2np7-jv14][PSI-102 · doi:10.60555/gd4k-8h62].

This testing matters because buoyancy affects microgravity smoke properties, causing space fires to produce different particle sizes than Earth fires [A Researcher's Guide to International Space Station Combustion Science (2015) · nasa.gov/missions/station/a-researchers-guide-to-combustion-science]. Data from SAME provides reduced-gravity baselines to build rapid fire detectors with fewer false alarms for future long-duration spaceflight [A Researcher's Guide to International Space Station Combustion Science (2015) · nasa.gov/missions/station/a-researchers-guide-to-combustion-science][PSI-102 · doi:10.60555/gd4k-8h62][PSI-101 · doi:10.60555/2np7-jv14]. These advanced detectors can also save lives in extreme Earth environments like submarines [PSI-102 · doi:10.60555/gd4k-8h62][PSI-101 · doi:10.60555/2np7-jv14].

question: What gases were used to put out flames, and in which experiment?
answer:
In the Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX), researchers planned to measure the effectiveness of gaseous fire suppressants including carbon dioxide (CO2), helium (He), and sulfur hexafluoride (SF6) [PSI-69 · doi:10.60555/mbq8-0451]. Additionally, in the CFI experiment, fuels were diluted with helium, atomic nitrogen, and molecular oxygen to study their influence on flame extinction [PSI-39 · doi:10.60555/m6pj-a914]. 

Our sources do not cover experimental result data showing which specific gases successfully put out flames in completed tests [PSI-39 · doi:10.60555/m6pj-a914][PSI-69 · doi:10.60555/mbq8-0451].

question: What happened in the Mir fire in 1997, and what was learned?
answer:
On February 24, 1997, a fire ignited in a solid fuel oxygen generator in the Kvant-1 module aboard the space station Mir [25 Years Ago: Fire Aboard Space Station Mir · nasa.gov/history/25-years-ago-fire-aboard-space-station-mir]. The searing flame lasted several minutes, blocked access to one of two Soyuz escape vehicles, and filled station modules with toxic smoke [25 Years Ago: Fire Aboard Space Station Mir · nasa.gov/history/25-years-ago-fire-aboard-space-station-mir]. The six crew members extinguished the flames despite narrow confines, causing no structural damage to Mir [25 Years Ago: Fire Aboard Space Station Mir · nasa.gov/history/25-years-ago-fire-aboard-space-station-mir]. The station's life support system cleared the toxic smoke over several hours, and the crew suffered no lasting harm [25 Years Ago: Fire Aboard Space Station Mir · nasa.gov/history/25-years-ago-fire-aboard-space-station-mir]. Lessons learned from the incident were passed on to the design and operations of the International Space Station [25 Years Ago: Fire Aboard Space Station Mir · nasa.gov/history/25-years-ago-fire-aboard-space-station-mir]. 

Our sources do not cover specific technical root causes or detailed engineering modifications that resulted from the fire [25 Years Ago: Fire Aboard Space Station Mir · nasa.gov/history/25-years-ago-fire-aboard-space-station-mir].

question: Is there any fire data for Moon or Mars gravity?
answer:
The NASA Physical Science Informatics repository contains no real partial-gravity combustion data from investigations in actual Moon or Mars gravity [PSI Combustion Science coverage (24 investigations) · psi.nasa.gov/physci/repo/search?q=combustion]. However, cotton-fiberglass fabric flame behavior in lunar gravity has been simulated on Earth using a drop tower centrifuge [NASA Combustion Science · nasa.gov/glenn/glenn-expertise-space-exploration/physical-sciences-program/combustion-science]. The Flammability of Materials on the Moon (FM2) experiment is planned to test burning materials at 1/6 lunar gravity, but it is designated as an experiment to be performed in the future rather than completed data [NASA Combustion Science · nasa.gov/glenn/glenn-expertise-space-exploration/physical-sciences-program/combustion-science]. 

Our sources do not cover any real fire data collected directly on the surface of Mars or the Moon [PSI Combustion Science coverage (24 investigations) · psi.nasa.gov/physci/repo/search?q=combustion].

question: What are cool flames and why are they a risk?
answer:
Cool flames are lower-temperature flames that form as an intermediate step between unreacted fuel and oxidizer [A Researcher's Guide to International Space Station Combustion Science (2015) · nasa.gov/missions/station/a-researchers-guide-to-combustion-science]. They can form after a visible hot flame extinguishes and continue to burn a fraction of vaporized fuel for a prolonged period of time [A Researcher's Guide to International Space Station Combustion Science (2015) · nasa.gov/missions/station/a-researchers-guide-to-combustion-science]. Researching cool flames helps refine knowledge of low-temperature combustion, ignition phenomena, and engine design [PSI-39 · doi:10.60555/m6pj-a914][A Researcher's Guide to International Space Station Combustion Science (2015) · nasa.gov/missions/station/a-researchers-guide-to-combustion-science]. Additional tests aboard the International Space Station are planned to demonstrate cool flame behavior across various pressures and fuels [PSI-159 · doi:10.60555/cyt1-kh64]. 

Our sources do not explicitly detail why cool flames are a specific risk, beyond noting their persistent burning after visible flame extinguishment and their relevance to microgravity spacecraft fire safety [PSI-39 · doi:10.60555/m6pj-a914][A Researcher's Guide to International Space Station Combustion Science (2015) · nasa.gov/missions/station/a-researchers-guide-to-combustion-science].
